articles.title: New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors
articles.summary: A major breakthrough in superconductivity research has revealed that one of the essential ingredients for electricity to flow without resistance can exist at room temperature. Scientists discovered that electrons can form stable pairs at much higher temperatures than previously understood, suggesting that a different obstacle may be preventing room-temperature superconductivity.
articles.content:
Imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency. Superconductivity could help make these technologies possible, but a major challenge has stood in the way for more than a century. Most superconducting materials function only when cooled to extremely low temperatures, making widespread use costly and complicated.

Now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an important clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature. Their findings, published in the journal Science, reveal that one of the essential requirements for superconductivity can already be satisfied without extreme cooling. The discovery offers a promising new direction in the search for materials that conduct electricity without resistance.

To understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster. When electricity passes through its metal heating element, electrical resistance causes the wire to heat up and glow red, producing the heat needed to toast bread.

That resistance is useful for cooking, but in most electrical systems, it creates unwanted energy losses. Even something as simple as charging a phone involves some electricity being converted into heat rather than being put to useful work.

Why Superconductivity Requires Extreme Cold

Superconductivity eliminates this problem by allowing electrical current to move through certain materials with zero resistance. In principle, this could dramatically improve the efficiency of electrical systems and enable technologies that are difficult or expensive to operate today.

The challenge is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C using liquid helium before they exhibit this remarkable behavior. Maintaining such extreme conditions requires substantial energy and expensive cooling equipment, limiting practical applications.

Superconductivity was first observed in 1911. Decades later, in the mid-1980s, researchers discovered a new class of materials that could become superconducting at much warmer temperatures, around -173°C. Although still extremely cold, this represented an important advance.

However, these materials introduced a major scientific mystery. The established theory that successfully describes conventional, low-temperature superconductivity could not explain how the newer materials worked. Despite decades of research, the mechanisms behind high-temperature superconductivity remain poorly understood.

"We don't understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all," says Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. "And if you don't understand it, you can't systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal."

A Crucial Ingredient Works at Room Temperature

The new study provides an important piece of the puzzle. Swart and his colleagues have demonstrated that one of the two fundamental conditions needed for superconductivity can exist even at room temperature.

"This is really good news," says Swart. "We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren't possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether."

The finding suggests that scientists may need to focus less on whether electrons can form the necessary connections and more on how those electrons coordinate their behavior.

The Secret Lies in How Electrons Move Together

Superconductivity depends on two essential processes. First, electrons must join together in pairs called Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated way, maintaining a shared quantum state that allows electrical current to flow without resistance.

An analogy is a dance floor filled with ten couples. Having each couple dance together is only the first step. For the entire group to move as one, all ten couples must also coordinate their movements.

In conventional superconductors, electron pairing and this collective coordination emerge at the same temperature. The new findings show that high-temperature superconductors behave differently. Their electrons can form pairs at temperatures substantially higher than those needed for superconductivity itself to appear.

Even more remarkably, the researchers found that these pairs can remain intact at room temperature.

"The 'glue' that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature," says Swart. "This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck."

Phase coherence describes the coordinated quantum behavior of the electron pairs. Without it, the pairs may exist, but the material does not become superconducting. This suggests that achieving and maintaining that coordination could be the crucial remaining challenge.

"If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures."

Swart intends to investigate this process in future research, with the goal of understanding how superconductivity might be sustained at increasingly warmer temperatures.

New Technology Reveals a Hidden Superconductivity Clue

The breakthrough was made possible by specialized measurement equipment designed and constructed by the research team.

Unlike conventional measurement approaches, the new instruments could distinguish electrical current flowing through individual electrons from current carried by paired electrons. This allowed the researchers to examine when electron pairs formed and how they behaved inside the material.

By separating these two contributions, the team gained a clearer picture of the processes underlying high-temperature superconductivity and identified where a critical obstacle may lie.

The findings do not mean that room-temperature superconductivity has been achieved. They do, however, demonstrate that one of its essential ingredients can survive under everyday temperature conditions. Understanding how to make those electron pairs act together could bring scientists closer to a long-sought breakthrough in electrical technology.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in understanding a key mechanism related to room-temperature superconductivity, which has broad implications for energy efficiency and advanced technologies. The discovery that electron pairs can exist at room temperature is a major step toward overcoming a century-old challenge, with potential large-scale benefits for society. The article provides detailed context, explains the significance, and focuses on a single important topic.

articles.title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave
articles.summary: Europe hopes to be a leader in a new generation of computer chips which use light to process data.
articles.content:
"Photonic chips are on the verge of a breakthrough," says Ton van Mol of the Dutch research institute TNO.

If van Mol is right – and TNO, the European Union and the Dutch government are backing the idea with millions of euros - then the technology could be a gamechanger.

The chips which run today's society, from your phone and TV, to the vast data centres meeting our insatiable desire for AI, are mostly electrical.

They process data by shunting electrons around tiny circuits – a single microchip produced today can contain billions of transistors, and sizes are measured in nanometres (one nanometre is a billionth of a metre).

Because they use light instead of electricity, photonic chips are faster, use less energy and generate less heat than traditional computer chips.

Van Mol hopes for an acceleration in photonics similar to the one seen in electrical chips since the 1970s.

"With optical chips, you are now where electronic chips were maybe 40 [or] 50 years ago."

American, Taiwanese and Chinese firms dominate the computer chip industry, but Europe sees the emergence of photonic chips as a fresh opportunity to lead, on what could be, a key future technology.

Which is why the European Union has committed €400m ($450m; £330m) to a project called PIX Europe, external, with the stated goal of making the continent "a global leader in emerging technology for Photonic Integrated Chips".

"Europe said 'we need to have our own manufacturing in-house'," says van Mol, who is leading a key part of the programme.

"We cannot depend like in the past that everything is manufactured in the US or China - that's not wise, so the [European] Chips Act was called into life, and one of the parts of the act is to build pilot lines to really bring the technology, which is now in labs, to the next stage - manufacturing."
articles.reasoning: The article describes a significant European initiative to develop photonic chips, a breakthrough technology that uses light to process data faster and more efficiently than traditional electronic chips. This has broad implications for the future of computing, energy efficiency, and technological leadership, benefiting society at large. The EU's substantial investment and strategic focus on manufacturing independence add to the story's significance and substance.

**What happened** – The European Union, along with Dutch research institute TNO and the Dutch government, is investing €400 million in a project called PIX Europe. This project aims to develop photonic chips and create factories to make them in Europe. Ton van Mol from TNO explained that photonic chips are at a stage similar to where electric chips were 40 to 50 years ago, meaning there is room for big progress.

**Impact** – If successful, Europe could become a leader in this new technology, reducing its reliance on chip makers from other countries. articles.title: We now know how radiation destroys electronics devices
articles.summary: A detailed picture of how a single particle of radiation can destroy a semiconductor device could offer pointers for how to make electronics more resilient to the harsh conditions of space
articles.content:
A detailed picture of how a single particle of radiation can destroy a semiconductor device could offer pointers for how to make electronics more resilient to the harsh conditions of space

Electronic circuit board Mentor57/Shutterstock

Researchers are gaining a new understanding of exactly how radiation destroys electronics devices. The work is a step towards building more resilient electronics for use in nuclear fusion experiments or in space.

Cristyan Quiñones at North Carolina State University stayed up for nearly three days so he could watch a beam of heavy ions destroy an array of electronics devices. It was a high-stakes experiment: few labs around the world operate heavy ion beams and securing access to run experiments is difficult. But it is only with experiments like this that researchers can systematically study the dangers that electronics devices would encounter on board a satellite or near a nuclear reactor.

In those challenging high-radiation environments, electronics devices can dramatically and rapidly fail during what is called “single-event burnout” (SEB). Thanks to their experiments, Quiñones and his colleagues have now zeroed in on exactly how SEB happens.

Advertisement

The researchers focused on electronics components called diodes that they built from aluminium nitride, a semiconductor made from aluminium and nitrogen. Similar diodes are used to help power electronics devices, and aluminium nitride has been put forward as a promising foundation for the next generation of such power components.

Researchers have also theorised that aluminium nitride is resilient to radiation exposure, which would make it a good choice for use in high-radiation environments such as space. But this idea has not been thoroughly investigated in experiments, says team member Ramón Collazo, also at North Carolina State University.

Optical microscope images of an irradiated diode before and after a SEB event Cristyan Quiñones, NC State University

In the new experiment, which also involved researchers from NASA, energetic ions of silver, gold or the rare earth metal praseodymium hit and entered each aluminium nitride diode, and the researchers tracked how much electric voltage the diode could then sustain before SEB destroyed it.

Through data analysis and computer simulations, they found that each ion caused a disturbance within the diode, which, combined with the voltage, created a localised electric field. At some threshold voltage, that field became strong enough for nearby electrons to flock towards it, and this avalanche of electrons onto the small area led to a miniature explosion.

Microscope images from the experiment clearly showed tiny, melted craters in the aluminium nitride diode where SEB happened in this way. Additionally, comparing aluminium nitride to similar semiconductors, the team determined that it could withstand higher electrical fields before exploding, but relatively low voltages. Such a systematic and careful comparison had not been done before, but will inform how the material is used going forward.

Understanding SEB is important because it is among the biggest challenges for making electronics reliable in space, says Ronald Schrimpf at Vanderbilt University in Tennessee, who wasn’t involved with the experiment. He says that power systems are often the most vulnerable part of an overall spacecraft, with phenomena like SEB occurring even when there are physical shields to protect electronics, so studying proposed power device materials that are potentially more resilient, like aluminium nitride, is timely. “If your power supply goes down, nothing works, right?” says Schrimpf.

While radiation-resilient electronics are important in nuclear engineering and a variety of other settings, including the technology used in radiation therapy for cancers, they have recently gained more attention because of proposals to put data centres into space. But Schrimpf says that making electronics ready for space is a complex scientific problem that also involves logistical challenges because the facilities for testing electronics materials, such as the ion beam in the new experiment, are scarce. For Collazo, uncovering physical processes such as the electron avalanche in aluminium nitride is key for innovation in this area.

“Cristyan is telling us the physics of what is happening. You can now design the device around it because you know what is actually causing the problem,” he says. The researchers are now working on developing design principles based on what they have learned about SEB so far, says Collazo.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in understanding how radiation destroys semiconductor devices, which has broad implications for improving the resilience of electronics used in space and nuclear environments. The research provides detailed experimental evidence and insights that can lead to better design of radiation-hardened electronics, benefiting space exploration, nuclear fusion, and potentially medical technologies. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights a meaningful advancement with wide-ranging positive impact.
articles.personality_title: Scientists reveal how radiation damages electronics to build tougher devices

articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques dévoilent comment les radiations endommagent l’électronique pour créer des appareils plus résistants
